title: NDT methods: what VT, PT, MT, ET, RT and UT each find
goals: Say what each of the six main NDT methods finds, and on which materials
Pick a method for a part from its material, the flaw's likely place and shape, and the access
Put the steps of a penetrant test in order
Say why planar flaws suit UT and volumetric flaws suit RT
summary:
**Non-destructive testing** (NDT) finds flaws without damaging the part. Six methods do most of the work:

- **VT, visual**: always first. Surface only. Good light, magnifiers, borescopes.
- **PT, penetrant**: a dye soaks into flaws **open to the surface**, then a developer draws it out. Any non-porous material, magnetic or not. Steps: clean, penetrant (dwell), remove excess, developer, inspect, clean.
- **MT, magnetic particle**: a magnetic field leaks out at a flaw and gathers iron particles. **Ferromagnetic** materials only (not austenitic stainless, aluminium, titanium). Surface and just below (a millimetre or two). Finds flaws best **across** the field, so test in two directions about 90° apart.
- **ET, eddy current**: a coil induces currents in a **conductive** material; a crack disturbs them. Surface and near-surface cracks, conductivity, coating thickness, tubes. No couplant, fast.
- **RT, radiography**: X-rays or gamma rays through the part onto film or a detector. Shows **volumetric** flaws (porosity, slag) well; cracks only if lined up with the beam. Needs access to both sides and radiation safety.
- **UT, ultrasonic**: sound pulses reflect from flaws and the back wall. **Internal** flaws, especially **planar** ones (cracks, lack of fusion) facing the beam; thickness. One-side access; needs couplant.

**Choosing**: Is the material magnetic? Conductive? Is the flaw at the surface or inside? Flat (planar) or rounded (volumetric)? Which sides can you reach? Standards such as EN ISO 17635 give the choices for welds.

Planar flaws are the dangerous ones: they have sharp edges that grow. UT sees a flat reflector face-on; RT only sees it edge-on to the beam.

bench.task: Next time you see a weld or casting tested on site, note for each method used: what it was looking for, why that method, and what it could not have found.
check: Where the flaws of concern would be: surface or inside
Their likely shape: planar or volumetric
What another method would have added

cards.q: You need to check an austenitic stainless steel weld for surface-breaking cracks. Which method suits?
cards.why: Austenitic stainless is not magnetic, so MT will not work. PT finds anything open to the surface on any non-porous material. RT is poor at fine surface cracks unless they line up with the beam.

cards.title: Visual and penetrant: the surface
cards.body:
**VT** (visual) comes first, always: shape, cracks, undercut, corrosion, with good light and a magnifier or borescope.

**PT** (liquid penetrant) shows flaws **open to the surface** on any non-porous material, magnetic or not:

1. Clean and dry the surface
2. Apply penetrant and leave it to soak in (the **dwell time**)
3. Remove the excess from the surface
4. Apply developer, which draws penetrant back out of flaws
5. Inspect: red on white, or fluorescent under UV-A light
6. Clean off
cards.more:
PT is like spilling ink on a cracked tile, wiping the top clean, then dusting it with chalk: the chalk soaks the ink back out of the crack and shows a coloured line wider than the crack itself.

It cannot see anything that does not break the surface, and it needs the flaw to be clean and open: paint, grease or a smeared-over crack (from grinding) blocks it. That is why cleaning comes first and why surfaces are not ground just before testing.

Fluorescent penetrant under UV-A in a darkened booth is more sensitive than red dye in daylight.

cards.q: What can penetrant testing not find?
options: A crack that does not break the surface
Surface porosity in an aluminium casting
A fatigue crack at a bolt hole's edge
A surface crack in stainless steel
cards.why: Penetrant has to soak into an opening. Anything below the surface is invisible to it, however big.

cards.title: Magnetic particle: steel's surface and just below
cards.body:
**MT** magnetises the part (a yoke, a coil or current through it). Where a flaw cuts across the field, the field **leaks** out and gathers fine iron particles into a visible line.

- **Ferromagnetic** materials only: carbon and low-alloy steels, cast iron. Not austenitic stainless, aluminium, copper or titanium.
- Surface flaws, and ones a millimetre or two below it.
- Flaws show best when they lie **across** the field, so test twice, with the field turned about **90°**.
- Demagnetise afterwards where it matters.
cards.more:
Put a magnet under a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings: they gather where the field comes out. A crack in magnetised steel is a gap the field has to jump, so it bulges out of the surface there and the particles pile up over the crack.

A crack running **along** the field barely disturbs it, like a stick lying in a stream, and can be missed: hence the second test at right angles.

MT is faster and more sensitive than PT on steel, and works through thin paint, but it is no use on non-magnetic metals.

cards.q: Why is magnetic particle testing done twice, with the field turned about 90° the second time?
options: Flaws lying along the field barely show
To be sure the particles stick to the steel
The first test only magnetises the part
Standards require two operators to agree
cards.why: A flaw shows when it cuts across the field and makes it leak. One running parallel to the field hardly disturbs it, so a second direction catches those.

cards.title: Eddy current: conductive metals, fast
cards.body:
**ET** passes an alternating current through a coil held near the part. That induces **eddy currents** in any **conductive** material. A crack, or a change in the metal, disturbs them, and the coil's reading changes.

It finds surface and near-surface **cracks** (aircraft skins, bolt holes, heat-exchanger tubes), and measures **conductivity**, **coating thickness** and heat-treatment differences.

No couplant, no chemicals, quick, and it can be automated. It needs reference standards, and it does not reach deep.
cards.more:
Swirls of current go round under the coil like whirlpools in a stream. A crack is a wall in the stream: the swirls have to go round it, and the coil feels the difference.

The higher the frequency, the shallower the currents run (the skin effect): high frequency for fine surface cracks, lower frequency to reach a little deeper, through paint, or into a second layer.

Because it works through paint and needs no cleaning or couplant, ET is the favourite for in-service checks of aircraft and of tubes from the inside.

cards.q: Eddy current testing needs the part to be…
cards.why: Eddy currents can only flow in a conductor: aluminium, copper, titanium and steels all work. It does not need the part to be magnetic (that is MT), couplant (UT) or two-sided access (RT).

cards.title: Radiography: a shadow picture
cards.body:
**RT** sends **X-rays** or **gamma rays** (from a source such as iridium-192) through the part onto film or a digital detector. Thinner or less dense places let more through and show darker.

- Good for **volumetric** flaws: porosity, slag, shrinkage.
- **Cracks** and lack of fusion show only if lined up with the beam.
- Needs access to **both sides** (source one side, film the other).
- A permanent image to keep.
- **Radiation** needs controlled areas and trained people (in the UK, the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017).
cards.more:
It is a hospital X-ray of a weld. A gas pore is a bubble of nothing: less metal for the rays to cross, so a dark round spot.

A crack is a thin flat gap. If the beam runs along it (edge-on), the rays cross a long thin gap and you see a fine dark line. If the beam hits it face-on, the rays cross only the crack's tiny width: almost no change, and it can be missed.

So RT is great at counting porosity and poor at being sure there are no cracks: the opposite of UT.

cards.q: Why can radiography miss a crack?
options: Face-on to the beam, it barely changes the metal crossed
X-rays cannot pass through steel at all
Cracks are too dense to show on film
Radiography only finds flaws on the surface
cards.why: A crack is very thin. Seen face-on, the rays cross almost the same thickness of metal as next to it, so there is little contrast. Edge-on to the beam it shows.

cards.title: Ultrasonic: echoes from inside
cards.body:
**UT** sends short pulses of high-frequency sound into the part through a **couplant** (gel, oil, water). Echoes come back from the back wall and from anything in between.

- **Internal** flaws, and **thickness** (corrosion mapping).
- Very good at **planar** flaws (cracks, lack of fusion) that face the beam: angle probes are aimed to meet them square on.
- Access from **one side**; no radiation.
- Needs a skilled operator, a coupled surface, and calibration. **PAUT** (phased array) and **TOFD** record the scan.
cards.more:
Shouting into a cave and listening for the echo: the time tells you how far, the loudness something about the size.

A crack is a flat mirror for sound. Hit it square on and it sends back a strong echo; that is why weld inspectors use angle probes (45°, 60°, 70°), chosen so the beam meets the likely fusion faces at right angles.

UT and RT complement each other: UT for cracks and thickness, from one side; RT for porosity and a picture that anyone can look at later.

cards.q: A pressure vessel wall can only be reached from the outside. You need to find cracks deep inside the weld. Which method?
cards.why: UT works from one side and finds planar flaws deep inside. RT needs a film on the far side, PT sees only the surface, and ET does not reach deep into steel.

cards.title: Choosing a method
cards.body:
Four questions pick the method:

1. **Material**: magnetic (MT possible)? conductive (ET possible)?
2. **Where is the flaw**: open to the surface (VT, PT, MT, ET) or inside (UT, RT)?
3. **Its shape**: **planar**, flat like a crack (UT, MT, PT, ET), or **volumetric**, rounded like a pore (RT, UT)?
4. **Access**: one side (UT, ET, MT, PT) or both (RT)?

For welds, **EN ISO 17635** sets out which methods suit which materials and joints.
cards.more:
Work through a real job: a fatigue crack suspected at the toe of a fillet weld on a steel crane beam. Steel is magnetic. A toe crack breaks the surface. It is planar. One side is enough.

So: VT first, then MT (fast, sensitive, works through thin paint). PT would also work but needs the paint off. RT would struggle with a fine crack across the beam, and UT is possible but slower for a surface flaw.

Now change one thing: the beam is aluminium. MT is out; PT or ET instead.

cards.q: Match each job with a method that suits it.
pairs: Surface cracks on a mild steel weld
Surface cracks on an aluminium casting
Wall thickness of a corroded pipe
Cracks in heat-exchanger tubes, from inside
cards.why: Material, flaw place and shape, and access decide. Other methods could do some of these jobs; these are the usual first choices.

cards.q: Put the steps of a penetrant test in order.
items: Apply penetrant and wait the dwell time
cards.why: Clean first, or the penetrant cannot get in. Remove the excess before the developer, or the whole surface bleeds colour.

cards.q: On which of these does magnetic particle testing not work?
cards.why: MT needs a ferromagnetic material. Austenitic stainless (304, 316) is not, so use PT or ET. Ferritic steels and cast iron are fine.

cards.q: Sort each weld flaw: planar or volumetric?
cards.why: Planar flaws are flat with sharp edges, and tend to grow: UT finds them best. Volumetric flaws have depth in every direction: RT shows them well.

cards.front: MT: which materials, and how deep?
cards.back: Ferromagnetic only (carbon and low-alloy steels, cast iron). Surface and a millimetre or two below.

cards.front: ET: what does it need, and what is it good for?
cards.back: A conductive material. Surface and near-surface cracks, conductivity, coating thickness, tubes. No couplant; fast.

cards.q: You need to measure the thickness of paint on an aluminium panel. Which method?
cards.why: An eddy-current coating gauge measures the gap between the probe and the conductive metal, which is the paint thickness. MT needs magnetic metal; PT and RT do not measure coatings.

cards.q: Which method needs access to both sides of the part?
cards.why: RT puts the source on one side and the film or detector on the other. The others work from the side you can reach.

cards.q: Surface cracks are suspected on an aluminium alloy bracket. Which method would you choose first, after a visual check?
cards.why: Aluminium is not magnetic, so MT is out. PT finds surface-breaking cracks on any non-porous material. (ET would also do.)

cards.q: Match each method with what it relies on.
pairs: A dye drawn into surface openings
Magnetic flux leaking at a flaw
Induced currents disturbed by a flaw

cards.q: Why are UT and RT often used together on important welds?
options: UT is best at planar flaws, RT at volumetric
Each needs the other's results to calibrate
Neither can find any flaw on its own
RT measures thickness and UT finds porosity
cards.why: UT sees cracks and lack of fusion that face the beam, and RT gives a clear picture of porosity and slag. Together they cover each other's blind spots.
